title: Attention as prayer
hookLine: Simone Weil held that attention, taken to its highest, is prayer

lines: ATTENTION, AT ITS HIGHEST, IS PRAYER.
cards: A student sits over a geometry problem and can't crack it. The hour runs out. The page is a mess of crossed-out lines.

Was the hour wasted? Simone Weil, a French philosopher deeply drawn to Christ, said no. In an essay written for students, she argued that real effort of attention is never lost, even when the problem stays unsolved.
What's being trained, she said, isn't geometry. It's attention. And attention, taken to its highest, is the same thing as prayer.

teach.b: Weil means something specific by attention. Not frowning. Not clenching your jaw.
She describes it as more like waiting: holding your own thoughts back, empty and ready, so that what's really there can come in. Straining gets in the way.

That's why she cared about schoolwork. A Latin translation, a math proof: done with real attention, she thought, each one stretches the same capacity the soul uses to turn toward God. Then she turns it toward people.
Love of neighbor, Weil wrote, comes down to being able to ask someone, what are you going through? And then actually to look and listen, without rushing to fix them.
She thought that kind of attention was rare, and close to a miracle. Luke has a scene she'd recognize, one this path met earlier. Jesus is a guest in a home.
Martha is busy serving. Her sister Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word."

Martha complains, and Jesus answers: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part." Readers take this in different ways.
Some stress that Martha's work is good too, just anxious. Some hear Mary as a picture of prayer itself. Weil's lens adds one thing: Mary isn't doing nothing.
She's attending. A phone buzzing face-down on the table. A friend talking while you plan your reply.
A prayer said while thinking about lunch. Weil's point lands on all of them: the opposite of prayer may not be doubt. It may be distraction.

how: Some Christians practice prayer as attention, sitting quietly before God without words, or praying while giving full attention to a task or a person; Simone Weil's essays are read in many settings as a guide to this.

o: trying hard to focus until your jaw is clenched
a rule that prayer only counts when the room is silent
full, waiting attention, which at its height is prayer

games.q: attention as prayer — tap the pairs.
p: careful and troubled about many things

s: Weil said real attention means straining as hard as you can
she describes it as a kind of waiting: thoughts held back, empty and ready. straining gets in the way.
Weil thought an unsolved problem can still be worth the effort
the effort trains attention, and she says that is never lost.
in Luke, Jesus tells Martha that one thing is needful
"one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part."

games.q: you're sitting at Jesus' feet, listening, while your sister bustles in the kitchen and complains that you've left her to serve alone. what do you do?
o: argue it out in front of the guest.
games.why: Mary stays. when Martha complains, Jesus says Mary "hath chosen that good part." some readers stress that Martha's work is good too.

practice: Choose one sound in the room, a clock, traffic, the hum of a fridge, your own breathing, and listen to it only, without naming or explaining it.

When your mind slides off, notice where it went and come back without scolding; attention, for Weil, is a kind of waiting. If you pray, you can let this listening be your prayer, with no words at all.

wordCard.voice: Attention as prayer. Simone Weil's claim that attention, taken to its highest, is the same as prayer: open, waiting, and fully there, for God and for a neighbor.

orig.note: French, Weil's language: waiting. she ties attention to waiting; her letters and essays were gathered as Attente de Dieu, in English Waiting for God.

carryVoice: Your line: attention is prayer. Even an hour on an unsolved problem trains it. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God' (in Waiting for God)
